Practice Makes
Culture Visible

This week, Morning Meeting launches the 15-Minute Neuro-Regulated Morning Circle. Across four lessons, students will notice what is happening in their bodies, practice tools for regulation, strengthen belonging through shared stories, and choose an observable intention for what comes next.

Inside this week’s Culture Weekly: the complete August 31–September 4 Morning Meeting sequence, two fresh classroom-practice clips from August 27, the full attendance picture, the counselors’ 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding and Your Happy Place activities, the K–8 counselor-lesson roadmap, updated DBRC data, grade-team shout-outs, and the updated Culture Meeting schedule.

The Commitment

It started with a shared commitment

Our shared commitments give us the language. Daily routines help students experience those commitments. When students can regulate, connect, practice, commit, and transition with support, they are better prepared to participate in a Safe, Respectful, and Responsible learning community.

Morning Meeting

The 15-Minute Neuro-Regulated Morning Circle

This week’s Morning Meeting unit is a trauma-responsive Tier 1 circle designed to regulate the body before instruction begins. Every 15-minute lesson uses the same six-phase arc:

Regulate→Orient→Connect→Practice→Commit→Transition

The repeated structure gives students a predictable way to notice their internal state, use a regulation strategy, connect with others, practice a skill, name a commitment, and transition into learning.

Attendance follow-up process

Teachers should make the initial parent contact or attempt when a student begins accumulating absences. Once a student reaches five absences, the teacher should email the counseling team so counselors can follow up with the family and determine whether additional support or intervention is needed.

Early communication helps us respond before attendance concerns become more difficult to address.

Counselor’s Corner

Coping Skills: Grounding + Your Happy Place

🌟 5 Senses Grounding

Sometimes our feelings can feel really big. When we are worried, frustrated, angry, or overwhelmed, grounding can help us slow down, calm our bodies, and focus on what is happening right now.

Try the 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding Technique. Take a slow breath and notice:

  • 5 things you can SEE
  • 4 things you can HEAR
  • 3 things you can TOUCH
  • 2 things you can SMELL
  • 1 thing you can TASTE

You can use this strategy at school, at home, or anywhere you need a moment to reset.

This week’s challenge: Try the 5-4-3-2-1 technique when you notice yourself feeling upset, nervous, frustrated, or overwhelmed.

Remember: Grounding helps bring our attention away from overwhelming feelings and back to the present moment.

💭 Your Happy Place

Everyone has a place where they feel safe, calm, comfortable, or happy. Your happy place doesn’t have to be somewhere you can physically visit—it can be a place you imagine in your mind!

Create your happy place. Take a few slow breaths and imagine yourself in a place where you feel peaceful. Ask yourself:

  • What do I see?
  • What sounds do I hear?
  • What do I smell?
  • What do I feel around me?
  • What makes this place special to me?

Spend a few moments imagining yourself there while taking slow, steady breaths. If you have time, you could even draw your happy place or write about it! Your happy place could be your bedroom, a beach, your grandmother’s house, a favorite park, or even an imaginary place.

This week’s challenge: When you feel stressed, angry, worried, or overwhelmed, take a moment to close your eyes, take a breath, and visit your happy place in your mind.

Remember: You can carry your happy place with you wherever you go!

LiveSchool

Create the opportunity to earn it

LiveSchool is our schoolwide system for student incentives and rewards. Please do not routinely hand out food, candy, drinks, or other incentive items during the day simply because a student completed an assignment or met an expectation. Instead, use the item as something students can work toward through LiveSchool points:

“You can earn LiveSchool points for meeting this expectation.”
“Once you have enough points, you can use them to purchase the reward through the LiveSchool Store.”

If you already have reward items you would like students to earn, coordinate with the student’s homeroom teacher so the reward can be distributed at an appropriate time. The goal is simple: do not just give the reward—create an opportunity for students to earn it.

LiveSchool StoreTentative
